explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), says, "I will bless Your name forever and ever." He wears a crown, and he still calls God "…my God and King…" There's no retirement date on that praise.

explanations.answer: For the rest of his reign
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd pick that, since David was king (2 Samuel 5:3) and a reign sounds like a long time. But David doesn't put a term limit on it. He says, "I will bless Your name forever and ever." That runs way past any crown he'll ever wear.

David fought battles as king (2 Samuel 8:1), so that's a fair thing to think of. But he never says his praise ends when the fighting does. He says, "I will bless Your name forever and ever." Battles come to an end, but this praise doesn't have a finish line, friend.

Feasts and victories are natural times to cheer, so I get the guess. But David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), says, "Every day I will bless You, and I will praise Your name forever and ever." That means the plain Tuesdays count too. Even the Tuesday when nothing happens and the oven is making a weird noise.

That's right, and David says it himself: "Every day I will bless You, and I will praise Your name forever and ever." He doesn't wait for a parade. Every. Single. Day, friend. Ordinary days get praise too.

Yes, baker. David says, "One generation will commend Your works to the next, and will proclaim Your mighty acts…" He's picturing the news getting passed down, one group to the next. It's like a recipe handed down from one cook to the next, except this news is the best thing to pass along.

A household is a lovely picture, and families do pass things down. But David's words are, "One generation will commend Your works to the next…" He's looking across time, not just around one kitchen table. So the word that fits is generation.

Tribe is a reasonable guess for a king who ruled over Israel (2 Samuel 5:3). But David says, "One generation will commend Your works to the next…" He's looking at who comes after, not at who sits beside him. That's why the word is generation.

That's right. David writes, "They will proclaim the power of Your awesome deeds, and I will declare Your greatness." He doesn't just sit in the audience while others do the talking. He joins the choir himself.

Close, but look at what David says: "They will proclaim the power of Your awesome deeds, and I will declare Your greatness." Others proclaim, and then he adds his own voice. He isn't leaving the job to the crowd. This king is singing too.

I can see why you'd guess that, but David says the opposite. He writes, "The LORD is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion." Slow to anger, not quick. Me, I get cranky when a timer beeps early.
That's right, baker. David says the LORD is "…slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion." He's also gracious and compassionate. Slow to anger. I've got a lot to learn there.
That's it, friend. David says, "The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made." Look how big that circle is. David doesn't draw a smaller one inside it.

Understandable, since a lot of the Bible talks about God's people. But in this verse David says, "The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made." He doesn't say only. His words are all and all He has made.

explanations.answer: Only to those who praise Him
explanations.explanation: That one makes sense, since the psalm is full of praise. But David doesn't put a condition on it. He says, "The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made." The words he picks are all and all He has made.

People are the obvious guess, since people are the ones writing psalms. But David says, "All You have made will give You thanks, O LORD, and Your saints will bless You." Look at that wording. The thanks comes from all He has made, and then the saints are named on top of that.

That's right, baker. David says, "All You have made will give You thanks, O LORD, and Your saints will bless You." The thanks comes from all He has made, and the saints are mentioned too. David's circle keeps getting wider.

explanations.answer: So people would know His mighty acts
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. David says they will speak of the glory of God's kingdom "…to make known to men Your mighty acts and the glorious splendor of Your kingdom." The talking has a job. It's about people getting to know what God has done.

explanations.answer: So His enemies would be afraid
explanations.explanation: I see where that comes from, since a mighty king sounds scary. But the psalm never says that here. David says the telling is "…to make known to men Your mighty acts and the glorious splendor of Your kingdom." The purpose he gives is that people would know.

explanations.answer: So God would reward the speakers
explanations.explanation: That's a natural thought if you're picturing a bonus for good work. But David never says anything about a reward in this verse. He says it's "…to make known to men Your mighty acts and the glorious splendor of Your kingdom." The point is people knowing, not the speakers collecting.
You got it, baker. David says, "Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures through all generations." Kingdoms usually have an end date. This one doesn't.

David was a king on earth (2 Samuel 5:3), so it's easy to think that way. But he says, "Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures through all generations." He doesn't call it earthly. He says it lasts.

Growing is a nice word for a kingdom. But that isn't the word David uses. He says, "Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures through all generations." What he says about it is that it's everlasting and endures.

Right on, baker. David says, "The LORD is faithful in all His words and kind in all His actions." All His words, not most of them. Most of us keep our word right up until the snooze button gets involved.
Hold on, that's not what David says. He writes, "The LORD is faithful in all His words and kind in all His actions." The word is all, not some. No fine print here, friend.

explanations.answer: He holds them up and lifts them
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. David says, "The LORD upholds all who fall and lifts up all who are bowed down." The word is all, and the LORD does the lifting. I've fallen off the counter plenty, and a hand like that sounds mighty good.

explanations.answer: He waits for them to stand alone
explanations.explanation: Plenty of us have felt like we're left to get up on our own. But David says, "The LORD upholds all who fall and lifts up all who are bowed down." He doesn't wait for them to stand alone. He holds them up and lifts them.

explanations.answer: He sends someone else to help
explanations.explanation: Helpers are good things, and I'd be a mess without mine. But David says, "The LORD upholds all who fall and lifts up all who are bowed down." The one doing the upholding and lifting is the LORD Himself.

Yes, baker. David says, "The eyes of all look to You, and You give them their food in season." Food in season means the right food at the right time. I wish my cookie orders showed up that well timed.

Rain makes sense for a land full of fields. But it isn't what this verse says. David says, "The eyes of all look to You, and You give them their food in season." What the LORD gives here is their food in season.

Rest is a gift, and I wouldn't say no to some. But David doesn't mention it in this verse. He says, "The eyes of all look to You, and You give them their food in season." The gift here is food, at the right time.

That's a common worry, that kindness has to be earned. But David says, "The LORD is righteous in all His ways and kind in all His deeds." He never adds a condition about earning it. The kindness is in all His deeds.

That's right, baker. David says, "The LORD is righteous in all His ways and kind in all His deeds." He doesn't add a test to pass first. Earlier he even says, "The LORD is good to all…" (Psalm 145:9).

explanations.answer: Those who call on Him in truth
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. David says, "The LORD is near to all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth." It's about calling out to Him, and doing it in truth. You don't need a fancy title or a special building.

The Sabbath mattered to God's people (Exodus 20:8), so that's a fair guess. But in this verse David says, "The LORD is near to all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth." What he names is calling on the LORD in truth.

explanations.answer: Those who serve in the temple
explanations.explanation: Serving in the temple sounds close to God, so I see why you picked it. But David doesn't say that here. He says, "The LORD is near to all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth." He names those who call out in truth.

explanations.answer: He hears them and saves them
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. David says, "He fulfills the desires of those who fear Him; He hears their cry and saves them." The LORD hears and the LORD saves. I know a little about crying out from the back of a dark junk drawer where I sat for years, and this verse hits home.

explanations.answer: He tests them a while longer
explanations.explanation: Waiting through hard times can feel like a test, so I understand that guess. But David says, "He fulfills the desires of those who fear Him; He hears their cry and saves them." The verse says the LORD hears and saves.

explanations.answer: He tells them to wait quietly
explanations.explanation: That one sounds sensible, since waiting is a big part of life. But this verse doesn't say it. David says, "He fulfills the desires of those who fear Him; He hears their cry and saves them." The words are hears and saves.

I can see the guess, since this psalm is so full of kindness. But David draws a line here. He says, "The LORD preserves all who love Him, but all the wicked He will destroy." This is a heavy verse, and it names two different outcomes.
That's right. David says, "The LORD preserves all who love Him, but all the wicked He will destroy." The two groups are not treated the same. It's a heavy line, and it's good to take it seriously.

Yes, baker. David ends with, "let every creature bless His holy name forever and ever." Every creature, not just the ones with a speaking part. And look at those last words. They're the same ones he started with.

A nation would be a big crowd, so I see why you picked it. But David's last line says, "let every creature bless His holy name forever and ever." He's calling on every creature, which is a bigger circle than any one nation.

Priests are the ones we picture leading worship, so that's a sensible guess. But David ends with, "let every creature bless His holy name forever and ever." He isn't naming one small group to do the praising. He calls on every creature.
